title: Reference frames, GPS clock example and inertial frame
sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: However, at the turn of the 20th century, two major concepts improved our understanding of nature. In 1900 Planck provided the basic ideas that led to the quantum theory, and in 1905 Einstein formulated his special theory of relativity. These theories inspired new developments and theories in the fields of atomic, nuclear, and condensed-matter physics.
For your information — GPS

According to relativity theory, a moving clock appears to run slow with respect to a similar clock that is at rest. The satellites are constantly moving relative to observers on the Earth which causes them to run at slightly faster rate than clocks on the Earth’s surface.

A calculation using General Relativity predicts that the clocks in each GPS satellite should get ahead of ground-based clocks by 45 microseconds per day. So the role of special theory of relativity is important in GPS.
18.1 REFERENCE FRAMES
A coordinate system in which an experimenter makes position and time measurements of physical events is called a reference frame.

In the theory of special relativity, an event, is a physical “happening” that occurs at a certain place and time. To record the event, experimenter uses a reference frame that consists of a set of x, y, z axes (called a coordinate system) and time measuring device such as a clock. Reference frames are used to specify the relationship between a moving observer and the event. However, in some physical situations, it is impractical to choose a reference system with a fixed origin.

Consider, for example, a jet plane landing on an aircraft carrier that is going forward at full throttle at the same time as shown in figure 18.1. You want to describe the plane’s motion in a coordinate system fixed to the carrier, even though the carrier is moving. The reason why this is important is that the plane needs to come to rest relative to the carrier at some fixed location on the deck.
A. Inertial Reference Frame
An inertial frame is one in which an object subjected to no forces moves in a straight line at constant speed.

sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: B. Non-inertial Reference Frame
An accelerating frame of reference is called a non-inertial frame of reference.
Any frame or system moving with constant velocity with respect to an inertial system must also be an inertial, thus there is no single, preferred inertial frame, as shown in figure 18.2

The earth-based reference frame is not exactly an inertial reference frame because it is subjected to centripetal acceleration as the earth spins on its axis and revolves around the sun. In most situations, the effects of these accelerations are small, and we can neglect them. Therefore the earth’s surface can be considered as inertial reference frame in many situations.

For example, when analyzing the motion of a cricket ball, the fact that Earth rotates about its axis does not have much effect. But if we want to analyze the motion of a meteor falling from a great distance toward Earth, Earth’s rotation must be considered.
18.2 SPECIAL THEORY OF RELATIVITY
In 1905 Albert Einstein proposed a theory that completely changed our views of space and time. He based his special theory of relativity on two postulates
1. The principle of relativity: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames.

The first postulate declares that the laws of physics are absolute, universal, and the same for all inertial observers. Laws that hold for one inertial observer cannot be violated for any inertial observer. Einstein’s principle of relativity means that any kind of experiment—mechanical, thermal, optical, or electrical—performed in a laboratory at rest must give the same result when performed in a laboratory moving at a constant speed past the first one.
For example the pouring of tea in an aeroplane moving with constant speed is same as that on earth.

2. The principle of constancy of the speed of light: The speed of light in a vacuum has the same value, c = 2.997 924 58 × 10⁸ m/s, in all inertial reference frames, regardless of the velocity of the observer or the velocity of the source emitting the light.
The second postulate is more difficult to accept because it seems to go against our ‘common sense,’ which we observe in everyday experiences.

Consider two experimenters one at torch A and the other at torch B as shown in figure 18.3. Both these experimenters, regardless of if they are at rest or move with respect to each other finds that in every situation light travel with the same speed as c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
18.3 CONSEQUENCES OF SPECIAL THEORY OF RELATIVITY
As we examine some of the consequences of relativity, we will find that they contradict some basic concepts.
A. SIMULTANEITY

Two events that are simultaneous in one frame are in general not simultaneous in a second frame moving with respect to the first. That is, simultaneity (the occurrence of two or more events at the same time) is not an absolute concept, but a relative concept that depends on the state of motion of the observer.

Einstein devised the following thought experiment to illustrate this point. A box car moves with uniform velocity, and two lightning bolts strike the ends of the box car, as shown in Figure 18.4, leaving marks on the boxcar and ground. The marks left on the box car are labeled A′ and B′; those on the ground are labeled A and B.

paragraphs: An observer at O moving with the box car is midway between A′ and B′, and a ground observer at O is midway between A and B. The events recorded by the observers are the light signals from the lightning bolts.

The two light signals reach the observer at O at the same time. This observer realizes that the light signals have traveled at the same speed over equal distances. Thus, observer O concludes that the events at A and B occurred simultaneously. Now consider the same events as viewed by the observer on the box car at O′. By the time the light has reached observer O′, observer O′ has moved. Thus, the light signal from B′ has already swept past O′, but the light from A′ has not yet reached O′.

According to Einstein, observer O′ must find that light travels at the same speed as that measured by observer O. Therefore, observer O′ concludes that the lightning struck the front of the box car before it struck the back. This thought experiment clearly demonstrates that the two events, which appear to O to be simultaneous, do not appear to be simultaneous to O′ as well.
B. TIME DILATION

The time taken for an event to occur within its rest frame is called proper time Δt_p. Observers in different frames in relative motion will always judge the time to be longer called time dilation Δt.
For your information — MATHEMATICAL PROOF OF TIME DILATION

Consider a vehicle moving to the right with a speed ‘v’ as in Figure. A mirror is fixed to the ceiling of the vehicle, and a laser at distance ‘d’ below the mirror’ emits a pulse of light directed toward the mirror, and at some later time after reflecting from the mirror, the pulse arrives back at the laser. Observer O′ at rest with the system measure the time interval Δt_p between these two events as
Δt_p = 2d / c        —①

Now consider the same set of events as viewed by O in a second frame. According to this observer, the mirror and laser are moving to the right with a speed ‘v’, and, as a result, the sequence of events appears different.

By the time the light from the laser reaches the mirror, the mirror has moved to the right a distance ‘vΔt/2’, where Δt is the time it takes the light pulse to travel from point A to the mirror and back to point A as measured by ‘O’. The Pythagorean theorem gives
(cΔt/2)² = (vΔt/2)² + d²
or   Δt = 2d / √(c² − v²)
Δt = 2d / (c√(1 − v²/c²))        —②
putting equation1 in equation 2 we get   Δt = Δt_p / √(1 − v²/c²)        —(B)

We can say that all physical processes, including chemical reactions and biological processes, slow down when observed from a reference frame in which they are moving. For example, the heartbeat of an astronaut moving through space would keep time with a clock inside the spaceship, but both the astronaut’s clock and her heartbeat appear slow to an observer, with another clock, in any other reference frame.
Science Tidbits — Twin Paradox

Suppose one of a pair of 20-year-old twins takes off in a spaceship traveling at very high speed to a distant star and back again, while the other twin remains on Earth. According to the Earth twin, the astronaut twin will age less.
C. LENGTH CONTRACTION

The length of an object measured within its rest frame is called proper length ΔL_p. Observers in different frames in relative motion will always measure the length to be shorter called length contraction ΔL.
D. RELATIVISTIC MASS
The mass of an object measured within its rest frame is called rest mass Δm_o. Observers in different frames in relative motion will always measure the mass to be greater called relativistic mass Δm.
E. MASS ENERGY EQUIVALENCE
The mass of an object is equivalent to certain quantity of energy, Thus mass can be converted into energy and conversely energy can be converted into mass. By the Einstein’s famous equation
E = Δmc²        (18.4)
In pair production of particle and antiparticle energy is converted into mass, whereas in particle annihilation with antiparticle the entire mass is converted into energy.

ALBERT EINSTEIN (1879-1955)

Albert Einstein was born on March 14, 1879 in Germany. In 1905, Einstein published three papers. The first was his explanation of the photoelectric effect. The second was on mathematical interpretation of Brownian motion. The third set out special relativity, revising our conceptions of time, length and energy. In 1933, he accepted a post at the Institute for Advanced Studies at Princeton (USA), where he stayed until his death on April 18, 1955.
APPLICATION OF TIME DILATION AND LENGTH CONTRACTION FOR SPACE TRAVEL

The special theory of relativity suggest that due to time dilation and length contraction effects our journey to distant places in universe will take less time. For example if a star is 8 light years away and we move to it in a spaceship with half the speed of light. From the point of view of spaceship-crew the length of the journey will be contracted.

EXAMPLE 18.1 — SPACE TRAVEL — Alpha Centauri is nearest star to our sun. It is at 4.37 light years from earth, it means that it takes 4.37 years for light to reach from earth to Alpha Centauri. If a spaceship is sent to Alpha Centauri with a speed of v = 0.96 c. How much time would have passed for the passengers, when they reach it? Assume that the earth and Alpha Centauri are stationary with respect to one another.
GIVEN — time for light to travel ‘t’ = 4.37 years, Speed ‘v’ = 0.96 c. REQUIRED — Proper time ‘t_p’ = ?
SOLUTION — The dilated time for person on earth is
Δt = 4.37 years / 0.96 = 4.55 years
The passenger on ship measures the proper time as
Δt_p = Δt × √(1 − v²/c²)
putting values   Δt_p = 4.55 years × √(1 − (0.96c)²/c²) = 4.55 years × √(1 − 0.92c²/c²)
therefore   Δt_p = 1.29 years   Answer
Thus, the passengers in spaceship will have aged only 1.29 years when they reach Alpha Centauri, and not the 4.55 years an observer on earth has calculated.

paragraphs: 18.4 BLACK BODY RADIATION
The electromagnetic radiation emitted by objects because of their temperature are called thermal radiation.

All bodies, no matter how hot or cold, continuously radiate electromagnetic waves. For example, we see the glow of very hot objects because they emit electromagnetic waves in the visible region of the spectrum. Our sun, which has a surface temperature of about 6000 K, appears yellow, while the cooler star Betelgeuse has a red-orange appearance due to its lower surface temperature of 2900 K. However, at relatively low temperatures, cooler objects emit visible light waves only weakly and, as a result, do not appear to be glowing. The human body, at only 310 K, does not emit enough visible light to be seen in the dark. However the human body does emit electromagnetic waves in the infrared region of the spectrum, and these can be detected with infrared-sensitive devices.
A perfect black-body at a constant temperature absorbs and re-emits all the electromagnetic radiation that falls on it.

A blackbody or perfect absorber is also an ideal radiator. In practice, a small opening in any heated cavity, behaves like a blackbody because such an opening traps all incident radiation. If the direction of the radiation is reversed in figure 18.6, the light emitted by a small opening is in thermal equilibrium with the walls, because it has been absorbed and re-emitted many times. The radiations emitted by black body are called black body radiations.
Science Tidbits — Glowing bolt

The glowing bolt in this picture radiates primarily in the infrared part of the spectrum, but it is hot enough (a few thousand kelvin) so that a significant portion of its radiation falls within the red end of the visible region. The other bolts are too cool to radiate any detectable amount of visible light.

The nature of the radiation from the cavity hole of black body depends upon the cavity walls. Experimental data for the distribution of energy of the black body at two different temperatures is shown in the figure. The radiation emitted (the area under the curve) increases by increasing temperature.
A. WEIN’S DISPLACEMENT LAW

With the increase in the wavelength the peak of distribution shifts toward shorter wavelength as in figure 18.6. This shift is found to obey Wien’s displacement Law. If ‘λ_max’ is the wavelength at which the curve peak and ‘T’ is absolute temperature then
λ_max ∝ 1/T   or   λ_max = Constant / T   or   λ_max T = Constant        (18.5)
Where constant = 0.2898 × 10⁻² m K.
B. STEPHEN-BOLTSMANN LAW

The area under the curve represents the total energy radiated per second per square metre over all wavelengths at particular temperature. It is found that area is directly proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature.
E ∝ T⁴   or   E = σ T⁴        (18.6)
Where the constant σ = 5.67× 10⁻⁸ Wm⁻²K⁻⁴ is called Stephen constant. And the relation 18.6 is called as Stephen-Boltsmann Law.

Several attempts were made to completely explain the black body spectrum, but all of them failed due to one reason or another. For example Raleigh-Jean presented a theory that could predict long wavelengths but was unable to predict short wavelengths. Similarly Wein presented a theory that explained short wavelengths but failed at longer wavelengths.

title: Photoelectric emission, stopping potential and two experiments
sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: 18.6 PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT
When light hits the metal surface electrons are emitted, the phenomena is called photoelectric effect and the electrons emitted are called photo-electrons.
When a beam of light having short enough wavelength is directed on a metal surface, the light will eject the electrons from the surface of metal, as shown in figure 18.10.

This phenomenon, was discovered by Heinrich Hertz in 1887, and Einstein explained it with photon concept of light in 1905. Let us analyze two basic photoelectric experiments, each using the apparatus shown in figure 18.10, in which light of frequency ‘f’ is directed onto metallic emitter and ejects electrons from it. A potential difference ‘V’ is maintained between metallic emitter and collector. This arrangement produces a photoelectric current ‘I’ that is measured with sensitive ammeter ‘A’.

First Photoelectric Experiment: We adjust the potential difference V by moving the sliding contact in figure 18.10 so that collector is slightly negative with respect to metallic emitter. This potential difference acts to slow down the ejected electrons. We then vary V until it reaches a certain value, called the stopping potential V_o, at which the reading of sensitive ammeter A has just dropped to zero.
When V = V_o, the most energetic ejected electrons are turned back just before reaching the collector. Then ‘KE_max’, the kinetic energy of these most energetic electrons, is
KE_max = eV_o        (18.9)
where ‘e’ is the elementary charge and V_o is the stopping potential.
Measurements show that for light of a given frequency, ‘KE_max’ does not depend on the intensity of the light.

The photoelectric current ‘I’ as a function of the potential difference ‘V’ for two different values of the intensity of the light is plotted in figure 18.11. When the intensity I is doubled, the current is doubled (twice as many photo-electrons are emitted), but the stopping potential V_o remains the same.

This experimental result is a puzzle for classical physics. Classically, the incident light is a sinusoidally oscillating electromagnetic wave. If we increase the amplitude of the wave, the electron should get a more energy as it is being ejected. That is not what happens.

Second Photoelectric Experiment: Now we vary the frequency f of the incident light and measure the associated stopping potential V_o or maximum Kinetic energy KE_max of photoelectrons. Figure 18.12 is a plot of KE_max versus f . Note that the photoelectric effect does not occur if the frequency is below a certain threshold frequency f_o (or equivalently, if the wavelength is greater than the corresponding threshold wavelength λ_o = c/f_o).

sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: This is another puzzle for classical physics. If we view light as an electromagnetic wave, we must expect that no matter how low the frequency may be, electrons can always be ejected by incident light if you supply them with enough energy—that is, if you use a light source that is bright enough. That is not what happens.

There is a third puzzle for classical physics in both experiments the wave theory predicts a time delay. However the first photoelectrons are emitted instantaneously after the light source is turned on.
EINSTEIN EXPLANATION OF PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT (PHOTON THEORY OF LIGHT)

Einstein used Planck’s concept of quantization of energy. Einstein proposed that the energy of electromagnetic radiation is not continuously distributed over the wave front, but instead is concentrated in localized bundles or quanta (also known as photons). The energy of a photon associated with an electromagnetic wave of frequency ‘f’ is
E = hf

Einstein’s picture was that a light quantum was so localized that it gave all its energy ‘hf’ directly to a single electron in the metal. Therefore, according to Einstein, the maximum kinetic energy for emitted electrons is
KE_max = hf − φ        (18.10)

where φ is the work function of the metal, which corresponds to the minimum energy with which an electron is bound in the metal. Table 18.1 lists values of work functions measured for different metals.
Table 18.1 Work Functions of Selected Metals
Metal — Work Function, Φ (in eV)

Equation 18.10 beautifully explain the puzzling independence of KE_max and intensity. For a fixed light frequency f, an increase in light intensity means more photons and more photoelectrons per second, although KE_max remains unchanged.

In addition, Equation 18.10 explain the phenomenon of threshold frequency f_o. Light of threshold frequency f_o, which has just enough energy to knock an electron out of the metal surface, causes the electron to be released with zero kinetic energy as shown in figure 18.13. Setting KE_max = 0 then f = f_o and Equation 18.10 gives
0 = hf_o − φ   or   hf_o = φ
hence   f_o = φ / h        —③
Thus the energy quantization used by Planck in solving the blackbody radiation problem was, in fact, a universal characteristic of light.
The general wave equation v = f λ in terms of threshold frequency f_o and the cut off wavelength λ_c can be written as
c = f_o λ_c   or   λ_c = c / f_o        —④
putting equation 3 in equation 4, we get   λ_c = hc / φ

Science Tidbits — Photocell
A device in which the photoelectric effect or photoconductivity is used to produce a current or voltage when exposed to light or other electromagnetic radiation.

A simple photocell is shown in the figure. It consist of evacuated glass tube with thin anode rod and cathode of appropriate surface. The material of cathode is selected whose work function suit the frequency of incident radiation on which the photocell is operated. When this surface is exposed to light electrons are emitted which are collected at cathode. As a result current flows in the external circuit. This current increases with intensity and stops when light beam is interrupted.

Burglar alarms and automatic doors often make use of the photocell circuit. When a person interrupts the beam of light, the sudden drop in current in the circuit activates a switch which operates a bell or opens the door. Photocells are used in many other devices, such as absorption spectrophotometers, to measure light intensity.

paragraphs: 18.7 COMPTON EFFECT
The scattering of high frequency photon strikes a stationary electron the frequency of photon is decreased after collision. This phenomenon is referred to as Compton’s effect.
EXPERIMENTAL ARRANGEMENT

The experimental arrangement of Compton effect is shown in the figure 18.14. A beam of X-rays having wavelength ‘λ’ is directed towards a target of graphite. The scattered photons have wavelength ‘λ′’ slightly longer, the amount of energy reduction depended upon the angle at which the X-rays were scattered.
The change in wavelength Δλ, between the scattered X-ray photon of wavelength λ′ and incident X-ray photon of wavelength λ is called Compton Shift.
The X-ray photon of frequency ‘f’ is incident on a stationary electron.
Arthur H. Compton (America). His work on X-ray scattering verified Einstein’s photon theory and earned him the 1927 Nobel Prize.

The initial energy of photon by Plancks theory is ‘hf’ and initial rest energy for electron by Eienstein equation is ‘m_oc²’. After collision the energy of photon reduce to hf ′ and electron is recoiled with total energy ‘mc²’ as shown in figure 18.15.
By law of conservation of energy
E_i,(photon) + E_i,(electron) = E_f,(photon) + E_f,(electron)
substituting values   hf + m_oc² = hf′ + mc²        —①

The initial momentum of photon is ‘hf/c’ and since electron is considered at rest therefore it have zero momentum. After collision the momentum of photon is ‘hf′/c’ making an angle ‘θ’ with its original direction and electron is recoiled with momentum ‘mv’ making an angle φ, as shown in figure 18.16.
By law of conservation of momentum
Along x-axis   P_ix,(photon) + P_ix,(electron) = P_fx,(photon) + P_fx,(electron)
substituting values   hf/c + 0 = (hf′/c) cosθ + mv cosφ
or   hf/c = (hf′/c) cosθ + mv cosφ        —②
By law of conservation of momentum
Along y-axis   P_iy,(photon) + P_iy,(electron) = P_fy,(photon) + P_fy,(electron)

sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: 18.8 PAIR PRODUCTION

The creation of an elementary particle and its antiparticle, usually when a photon (or another neutral boson) interacts with a nucleus an electron and its antiparticle, the positron, may be created is called pair production.
γ → e⁺ + e⁻

Pair production is the process in which a photon is converted into matter in accordance with Einstein equation E = mc². A photon when passes near a nucleus it disintegrates into electron and positron pair as shown in figure 18.18. Positron has the same mass as electron but opposite charge.
A photon cannot create an electron alone, because this would violate law of conservation of charge. Thus to conserve charge a positron is created.

In pair production for any energy of incident photon an additional massive object (such as atomic nucleus) is required to carry some of momentum. Therefore to conserve momentum the presence of nucleus is required.
In order to create an electron positron pair a minimal of 2m_oc² is needed, the surplus energy is taken by electron and positron as their Kinetic energies.
hf = 2m_oc² + (KE)₋e + (KE)₊e        (18.12)
For minimum energy the electron and positron will not carry any additional energy as their kinetic energies. Thus (KE)₋e and (KE)₊e must be zero, therefore the minimum energy is
hf = 2m_oc²
The rest mass of electron m_o = 9.11× 10⁻³¹ kg and speed of light c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s
Pair production requires at least 1.02 MeV energy photon. The photon in pair production will have a very short wavelength and very high frequency (as with X-ray and gamma-ray photons).
18.9 PAIR ANNIHILATION
When an electron (e−) and a positron (e+) collide two gamma ray photons are produced and the phenomenon is called pair annihilation.
e⁺ + e⁻ → γ + γ

When a positron and an electron combine together they annihilates as shown in figure 18.19. Both particles disappear, and two (or occasionally three) photons can appear, with total energy of at least. Decay into a single photon is impossible because such a process could not conserve both energy and momentum.
So each photon produced must have energy
hf = m_oc²
The rest mass of electron m_o = 9.11 10⁻³¹ kg and speed of light c = 3 10⁸ m/s
As with any two charged objects, electrons and positrons may also interact with each other without annihilating, in general by elastic scattering.

paragraphs: The electron-positron annihilation process is the physical phenomenon relied on as the basis of positron emission tomography (PET) and positron annihilation spectroscopy (PAS). It is also used as a method of measuring the Fermi surface and band structure in metals.
18.10 WAVE NATURE OF PARTICLES
Wave-particle duality is a theory that proposes that all matter exhibits the properties of not only particles, but also waves, which transfer energy.

Light and other electromagnetic radiation act sometimes like waves and sometimes like particles. Interference and diffraction demonstrate wave behavior, whereas in this chapter we saw considerable evidence for the photon theory of light as well, where electromagnetic waves consisted of photons, particle-like pulses that have energy and momentum.
DE-BROGLIE (1892-1987)
Louis de-Broglie (France). A member of an aristocratic family, his work contributed substantially to the early development of the quantum theory.

In 1924 a French physicist, Louis de-Broglie, made a remarkable proposal about the nature of matter. He reasoned that as light is dualistic in nature, behaving in some situations like waves and in others like particles. If nature is symmetric, this duality should also hold for matter. Electrons and protons, which we usually think of as particles, may in some situations behave like waves.

If a particle acts like a wave, it should have a wavelength and a frequency. De-Broglie postulated that a free particle with rest mass ‘m’, moving with non-relativistic speed ‘v’ should have a wavelength ‘λ’ related to its momentum ‘p= mv’ in exactly the same way as for a photon.
The energy of photon having frequency f by plancks theory is
E = hf        —①
According to Einstein mass energy relation   E = mc²        —②
comparing equation 1 and equation 2 we get   hf = mc²        —③
Dividing equation 3 by c we get   hf/c = mc²/c   or   hf/c = mc
Since momentum ‘P = mv’ for photon can be written for speed of light ‘c’ as ‘P = mc’ therefore
Equation 18.14 gives momentum of photon in terms of frequency, by general wave equation for light we also know that ‘c = fλ’, therefore equation 18.14 can be written as
hf/(fλ) = P   or   h/λ = P   hence   λ = h/P        (18.15)
Equation 18.15 gives momentum of photon in terms of wavelength.
De-Broglie argued that we can also assign wavelength to a particle of mass ‘m’ moving with velocity ‘v’ in the same way by putting ‘p = mv’
λ = h/mv        —④
If the particle’s speed is an appreciable fraction of the speed of light ‘c’, we can replace ‘mv’ in Equation 4 with
Thus in de-Broglie’s hypothesis, the relationships of wavelength to momentum and of frequency to energy are exactly the same for free particles as for photons.
DAVISSON AND GERMER EXPERIMENT
The Davisson-Germer experiment demonstrated the wave nature of the electron, confirming de-Broglie hypothesis.
An electron diffraction experiment gave the first experimental confirmation of the wave nature of particles (and the quantitative confirmation of the de-Broglie relationship λ = h/p).

title: Davisson–Germer electron diffraction and accelerated-electron wavelength example
sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: This experimental proof was provided by American physicists Clinton J. Davisson (1881-1958) and Lester H. Germer (1896-1971) at the Bell Laboratories in New York in 1927.

They designed a vacuum apparatus for measuring the energies of electrons scattered. The electron beam was accelerated towards nickel target, which could be rotated to observe angular dependence of the scattered electrons as shown in the figure 18.20. At certain angles there was a peak in the intensity of the scattered electron beam. This peak indicated wave behavior for the electrons, and could be interpreted by the Bragg law to give values for the lattice spacing in the nickel crystal.
The results obtained from the experiment were explained by treating electrons as waves of wavelength given by de Broglie’s equation.
The diffraction pattern of electrons from the nickel crystal was found similar to that of X-ray diffraction as shown in figure 18.21.

A similar demonstration of the wave nature of relativistic electrons was provided in the same year by G. P. Thomson, who observed the transmission of electrons with energies in the range of 10 to 40 keV through thin metallic foils (G. P. Thomson, the son of J. J. Thomson, shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1937 with Davisson).

The wave properties of particles like protons, neutrons, other atoms and even molecules has also been observed. In all cases the measured wavelengths agree with de Broglie’s prediction, proving that all matter has wavelike as well as particle like properties.
EXAMPLE 18.5 — ELECTRON WAVELENGTH — Determine the wavelength of electron that has been accelerated through a potential difference of (a) 50 V (b) 200 V.

GIVEN — Potential Difference ΔV₁ = 50 V; Potential Difference ΔV₂ = 200 V; rest mass of electron m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; Charge on electron q_e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; Plank’s constant h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ Js. REQUIRED — wavelength λ₁ = ?; wavelength λ₂ = ?
SOLUTION — The de-Broglie wave length λ is
λ = h / (m_e v)        —①
the speed of electron can be determined by its kinetic energy gained through the potential difference.
½ m_e v² = q_e ΔV   or   v² = 2q_e ΔV / m_e
Taking square root on both sides   v = √(2q_e ΔV / m_e)        —②

18.11 ELECTRON MICROSCOPE

An electron microscope (EM) is a type of microscope that uses an electron beam with its wave like properties to illuminate a specimen and produce a magnified image. Electron Microscope is based on the wave characteristics of electrons.

The resolving power of EM is greater than optical microscope because electrons have wavelengths about 100,000 times shorter than visible light photons. They can achieve better than 50 pm resolution and magnifications of up to about 10,000,000x (whereas ordinary, light microscopes are limited by diffraction to about 200 nm resolution and useful magnifications below 2000x).

The scanning electron microscope is shown in the figure 18.22, it produces images with a three-dimensional quality. The electron beam produced by an electron gun, is accelerated by an anode. The condenser lenses (electromagnetic coils) controls and defines the size of the electron beam (which set the resolution). The objective lens focus the beam onto the sample.

Two types of electrons used for imaging are Back Scattered Electrons (BSE) and Secondary Electrons (SE), which are collected by corresponding detectors. The X-rays generated from the electron-matter interaction is also collected through a detector. Computer is used to compile data from all the detectors and a magnified image of the object is obtained, as shown in figure 18.23.

sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: 18.12 THE UNCERTAINTY PRINCIPLE
This principle states that ‘the more precisely the position is determined, the less precisely the momentum is known in this instant, and vice versa’.

If a measurement of the position of a particle is made with precision ‘Δx’ and a simultaneous measurement of linear momentum is made with precision ‘ΔP_x’ the product of the two uncertainties can never be smaller than ‘h’, mathematically
Heisenberg (1901-1976)
Werner Heisenberg (Germany). Best known for the uncertainty principle, he also developed a complete formulation of the quantum theory based on matrices.

Suppose we design a super microscope and want to accurately measure the position and momentum of an electron at the same time as shown in figure 18.24. As objects can be seen to a precision of about the wavelength of the radiation used due for diffraction.
For us to see the electron and determine its location, at least one photon of light must strike the electron, however, the photon transfers some unknown amount of its momentum to the electron.

The incoming photon has momentum h/λ, in collision, the photon can transfer part (or all) of its momentum to the electron (along the x-axis). Therefore, the uncertainty in the electron’s momentum after the collision is as great as the momentum of the incoming photon, mathematically
ΔP_x ≈ h/λ        —①
Further, because the photon also has wave properties, we expect to be able to determine the electron’s position to within one wavelength of the light being used to view it, so
Δx ≈ λ        —②
multiplying equation 1 and equation 2 we get   Δx • ΔP_x ≈ λ × h/λ
and   Δx • ΔP_x ≈ h

paragraphs: The value ‘h’ represents the minimum in the product of the uncertainties. Because the uncertainty can always be greater than this minimum, we have
If ‘Δx’ is very small, then ‘ΔP_x’ is large, and vice versa.

Another form of uncertainty principle can be obtained through similar reasoning. The product of uncertainty in measurement of energy ‘ΔE’ and the time ‘Δt’ available for the measurement is approximately equal to the Planck’s constant.
Thus our knowledge about a particle is inherently uncertain. There will always be uncertainty in a particle about exact momentum at a given position and exact energy at a given time.

EXAMPLE 18.6 — UNCERTAINTY IN POSITION — An electron moves in a straight line with a constant speed 6.61 × 10⁶ m/s which has been measured to a precision of 0.10 %. What is the maximum precision with which its position could be simultaneously measured?
GIVEN — speed ‘v’ = 6.61 × 10⁶ m/s; mass of electron ‘m’ = 9.11 × 10-³¹ kg; precision percentage ‘%Δv’ = 0.10 %; Plank’s constant h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ Js. REQUIRED — position precision ‘Δx’ = ?
SOLUTION — The momentum ‘P’ of the electron is
P = mv
Putting values   P = 9.11× 10⁻³¹ kg × 6.61×10⁶ m/s
therefore   P = 6.02 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m/s
The momentum is ‘P = mv’, and the uncertainty in momentum ‘%ΔP’ is also = 10% which is ΔP = 0.0010 × P.
ΔP = 0.0010 × 6.02 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m/s   or   ΔP = 6.02 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m/s
From the uncertainty principle, the best simultaneous position measurement will have an uncertainty of
Δx • ΔP ≈ h
or   Δx ≈ h/ΔP   Putting values   Δx ≈ 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ Js / 6.02 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m/s
therefore   Δx ≈ 1.10 × 10⁻⁷ m   Answer
This is about 1000 times the diameter of an atom.

paragraphs: KEY POINTS
Inertial reference frame: a reference frame moving with constant velocity.
Non-inertial reference frame: a frame of reference that is accelerating.
Relativity: the study of how different observers measure the same event
Postulates os Special theory of relativity: the two postulates are
o The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames.
o The speed of light in free space has the same value for all observers, regardless of their state of motion
Black body: an ideal radiator, which can radiate equally well at all wavelengths
Quantized: the fact that certain physical entities exist only with particular discrete values and not every conceivable value
Plank’s Constant: h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ Js
Photon: a quantum, or particle, of electromagnetic radiation
Photo electric effect: the phenomenon whereby some materials eject electrons when light is shined on them
Compton effect: the phenomenon whereby x rays scattered from materials have decreased energy
Pair Production: the change of very high energy photon into electron -positron pair.
Annihilation of matter: when a positron comes close to an electron, they annihilate and produce two photons
de Broglie wavelength: the wavelength possessed by a particle of matter
Wave -particle duality: both radiation and matter exhibit particle as well as wave like properties
Heisenberg uncertainty principle: fundamental limit to the precision with which pairs of quantities (momentum and position, and energy and time) can be measured

paragraphs: 8. In a Compton scattering experiment at which angle the electron carry maximum energy? (Assume that initially the target electron is at rest). A. 0° B. 90° C. 135° D. 180°
9. If X-rays are scattered from protons instead of electrons, the change in its wavelength for a given angle of scattering A. increases B. decreases C. is unchanged D. is one radian
10. Pair production cannot take place in vacuum because. A. Mass is not conserved B. Momentum is not conserved C. Energy is not conserved D. Charge is not conserved
11. According to de-broglie equation which one has the smallest wavelength associated with it A. proton B. neutron C. α – particle D. electron

12. An electron and a proton have the same de-broglie wavelength. Then the kinetic energy of the electron is A. Zero B. infinity C. equal to the kinetic energy of the proton D. greater than the kinetic energy of the proton
13. In Electron microscope, light source is replaced by a beam of very fast moving A. electron B. neutron C. proton D. photon

14. According to Heisenberg, as the uncertainty in the measurement of a particle’s momentum is reduced by a factor of 2, by what factor is the uncertainty in that same particle’s position changed? A. 1/2 B. 1 C. 2 D. 4
CONCEPTUAL QUESTIONS
1. Imagine a world in which speed of light is only 50 m/s. How would the everyday events appear to us?
2. Some stars are observed to be reddish, and some are blue. Which stars have the higher surface temperature? Explain.
3. If the photo electric effect is observed for one metal, can you conclude that the effect will also be observed for another metal under the same conditions?
4. Does a light bulb at a temperature of 2500 K produce as white a light as the sun at 6000K?
5. A beam of red light and a beam of blue light have exactly the same energy. Which light contains the greater number of photons?
6. Why must the rest mass of a photon be zero?
7. Why don’t we observe Compton’s effect with visible light?
8. If an electron and a proton have the same de Broglie wavelength, which particle has greater speed?
9. An electron and a proton are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference. Which particle has the longer wavelength?
10. Why ultraviolet radiation is harmful to skin while visible light is not?
COMPREHENSIVE QUESTIONS
1. What are inertial and non-inertial reference frames? Explain with examples
2. State Einstein’s postulate of the special theory of relativity. Discuss its various results.
3. What are the main features of the thermal radiation from a black body? Discuss Planck’s quantum theory and its importance in physics.

title: Unit 18 comprehensive questions 4–9 and numerical problems 1–5
sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: 4. What is photoelectric effect? Discuss the failure of classical physics and success of photon concept in explaining this effect.
5. What is Compton’s effect? Develop a mathematical relation for the Compton’s wave shift.
6. Write note on pair production and annihilation of matter.
7. What is de Broglie hypothesis? Describe an experiment to show that particle has wave characteristics.
8. What is meant by wave-particle duality? Explain.
9. State and explain Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle. Justify the validity of this principle by a thought experiment.
NUMERICAL PROBLEMS
1. The length of a space ship is measured to be exactly one -third of its proper length. What is the speed of the space ship relative to the observer? (Answer: 0.9428c)

2. The time period of a pendulum is measured to be 3s in inertial frame of the pendulum. What is the period when measured by an observer moving with a speed of 0.95c with respect to the pendulum? (Answer: 9.6s)

3. A metal, whose work function is 3.0 eV, is illuminated by light of wavelength 3 × 10⁻⁷ m. Calculate the (a) threshold frequency, (b) maximum energy of photo-electrons and (c) stopping potential. (Answer: (a) 0.72 × 10¹⁵ Hz, (b) 1.16 eV (c) 1.16 V)
4. A 50 keV X-ray is scattered through an angle of 90°. What is the energy of X-ray after Compton Scattering? (Answer: 45.5 keV)
5. The speed of electron is measured to be 5 × 10³ ms⁻¹ to an accuracy of 0.003 %. Find the uncertainty in determining the position of this electron. (Answer: 4.84 × 10⁻³ m)
